days.title: Business Requirements: Functional vs Non-Functional, BCP, Cost, Integration, Data Movement and Disposition

concepts.heading: Functional and Non-Functional Requirements
concepts.body: A functional requirement says what the system does: save an address, refund a line item, export a picking list. A non-functional requirement (NFR) says how well it must do it and under which constraints: latency, availability, scalability, security, compliance, cost and operability. Architects spend most of their effort on NFRs because they decide regions, redundancy, data stores and spend, while functional items can usually be built on almost any platform. The key discipline is to make every NFR measurable before designing: 'fast' becomes a 95th percentile response time during promotions, 'always on' becomes an availability target for the whole customer request path. Words such as lowest or highest are not requirements: with no target every investment looks justified. When a product owner asks for the lowest latency worldwide, the highest availability and the lowest cost, these goals conflict (more regions and replicas cost more), so quantify each with the business, rank them, and record the agreement. The ranking decides which design wins when qualities collide. For example, EHR Healthcare's promise of at least 99.9% availability for customer-facing systems is an NFR that later drives zones, replicas and health checks.

concepts.heading: Business Continuity Planning and Tiering
concepts.body: Business continuity planning asks what the business must keep running, how long it can be without it, and how much recent data it can afford to lose. The starting tool is a business impact analysis (BIA), which ranks processes by the cost of interruption. From it you derive a recovery time objective (RTO, the longest acceptable outage) and a recovery point objective (RPO, the longest window of data that may be lost) for each system. Redundancy costs money in infrastructure and operations, so one strategy for everything either overspends on low-value systems or leaves the critical one exposed. The architect therefore tiers workloads and buys only the protection each tier needs. Take a parcel company where a dispatch outage stops revenue within minutes, the customer portal tolerates a few hours and the HR portal can be down for days: dispatch gets the tightest RTO and RPO, the portal a medium tier, HR a relaxed one. The detailed patterns (backup and restore, warm standby, hot) come after these targets are agreed, never before. Continuity requirements shape the design, so they cannot be deferred until after migration, and they are agreed with the business rather than chosen by each engineering team.

concepts.heading: Cost Trade-offs: TCO, Commitments and Attribution
concepts.body: The Well-Architected cost pillar frames cost as accountability and continuous monitoring. A fair business case compares the complete multi-year cost of both options on the same basis: on-premises means CapEx (hardware bought and depreciated) plus power, facility, network and staff, while cloud is mostly OpEx incurred as resources are consumed, plus support, networking and one-time migration, training and parallel-running effort. Sunk costs are ignored because the decision looks forward, and non-financial benefits such as agility are listed separately. For compute you can trade flexibility for discount. Resource-based committed use discounts commit to an amount of vCPUs and memory in one region and suit a steady footprint; flexible, spend-based commitments apply across eligible services and suit workloads that change machine series or region. Every commitment is paid whether used or not, so commit only to what is certain. For accountability, separate projects per team or consistent labels let billing reports and exports split spend by team, and Cloud Billing budgets with threshold alerts give early warning and can trigger automated responses. Disabling billing is a blunt reaction that takes down production.

concepts.heading: Integration Patterns and Moving Data
concepts.body: Integration patterns differ in how tightly they couple systems. Batch file transfer, such as nightly SFTP and ETL, is simple but latency is hours. Synchronous request and response is immediate, but the caller depends on every callee being up and fast, and each new consumer needs a producer change. Event-driven messaging lets producers publish events without knowing who reads them; consumers subscribe at their own pace, and new consumers are added without touching producers. Pub/Sub is the managed service for this. Cymbal Retail, with its SFTP and batch ETL integrations, is the typical case for moving to events. Data movement has its own choices. A one-time or periodic bulk copy is right for historical data. Change data capture (CDC) reads the source's change log and applies only inserts, updates and deletes, so a warehouse follows the source within seconds; Datastream is the serverless CDC service for sources such as MySQL, PostgreSQL, Oracle, SQL Server and MongoDB, replicating into BigQuery. For large file estates from on-premises storage to Cloud Storage, Storage Transfer Service with agents gives scheduling, retries, integrity checks and bandwidth throttling that ad hoc scripts lack.

concepts.heading: Disposition and Measuring Success with KPIs
concepts.body: For each capability the architect chooses a disposition: buy (SaaS or off-the-shelf), build, modify (extend or re-platform an existing system) or deprecate. Buying is fastest but means adapting to the product and depending on the vendor; building gives full fit with the highest cost, longest delay and permanent maintenance; modifying keeps familiar behaviour but carries technical debt forward; deprecating stops offering what no longer earns its cost. Drivers are time to value, team capacity, differentiation, integration needs and risk. KnightMotives wants CRM and dealer tools, carries technical debt and its dealers have no equipment budget, so a browser-based product integrated by APIs beats building: dealer CRM is a commodity, not a differentiator. Build only what makes the company different. To prove the decision worked, define KPIs: measurable outcomes with a baseline, a target and an owner. Outcome metrics such as monthly availability against the 99.9% target and unit cost per customer against the colocation baseline show whether goals were met; activity counts such as projects created or services migrated show effort, not result. ROI compares benefit to full cost while service quality is measured alongside.

examPoints: A question that gives a vague wish such as lowest cost and highest availability together is testing that NFRs must be quantified and ranked with the business before any design.
A question about workloads with very different outage impact is testing business impact analysis first, then per-system RTO and RPO tiers, never one uniform strategy.
A question about a commodity capability, stretched teams and a need for speed points to buy, while building is justified only where the capability differentiates the business.

quiz.q: A bank's new payments API is said to need 'near-zero downtime and instant responses at the lowest possible cost'. Architects disagree on whether to use multiple regions. What should the lead architect do first?
choices: Choose a multi-region deployment now, because availability and latency requirements always outweigh the cost concerns of a project
Convert each goal into a measurable target (latency percentile, availability percentage, cost ceiling), then rank them with the business
Pick the cheapest single-zone design now, because additional redundancy can always be added later without redesigning the data layer
Let each engineering squad pick its own targets, because the teams closest to the code know the true limits of the platform and its costs
quiz.explain: Vague goals cannot be designed against; measurable and ranked targets let the team defend a design and decide conflicts. Choosing multi-region first is tempting, but it fixes an expensive structure before anyone knows what the business values.

quiz.q: A hospital group wants to keep an on-premises PostgreSQL system serving patients while a reporting team in BigQuery sees changes within seconds. The team will not run replication servers. Which integration choice fits?
choices: Export the database to files every night and load them into BigQuery with a scheduled job
Have the application write each change to both databases so that the two stay identical at all times
Build a Compute Engine replication tool that polls every table for changes once each minute
Run Datastream change data capture from the source into BigQuery over a private connection
quiz.explain: Datastream is a serverless CDC service that reads the change log and replicates into BigQuery with low latency and no servers to run. The nightly export is tempting for simplicity, but the data would be a day old and the full exports load the live database.

days.recap: Quantify NFRs and rank them, run a business impact analysis to tier RTO and RPO, compare full multi-year TCO, decouple with Pub/Sub, use CDC (Datastream) or Storage Transfer Service for data, buy commodity capabilities and measure success with outcome KPIs.

days.title: Well-Architected Pillars, High Availability, Scalability and Latency Design

concepts.heading: The Well-Architected Pillars as a Trade-off Lens
concepts.body: The Google Cloud Well-Architected Framework organizes guidance into six pillars: operational excellence, security (with privacy and compliance), reliability, cost optimization, performance optimization and sustainability, plus cross-pillar perspectives such as AI and ML and financial services. On the exam the pillars are not a checklist to recite. They frame why one answer beats another. A design that is cheapest but ignores the stated availability target fails the reliability pillar; one that adds regions nobody asked for fails cost optimization. Read each scenario for the pillar that carries the stated requirement, then reject options that buy more of another pillar than the business asked for. Altostrat Media, for example, lists reliability and cost as top priorities, so the right design is the one that reaches the availability target with the least structural cost, not the maximum redundancy. Pillars also interact: autoscaling serves performance and cost together, and automation serves operational excellence and reliability. Perspectives add sector context, such as data residency requirements shaping the choice of fail-over region for financial services.

concepts.heading: Surviving a Zone Failure Automatically
concepts.body: A region contains several zones, which are separate failure domains. The reliability pillar says to build highly available systems through resource redundancy, and to handle failure automatically instead of by a person. Each tier needs capacity in more than one zone. A stateless tier uses a regional managed instance group, which spreads identical VMs over several zones; a load balancer stops sending traffic to unhealthy backends, so the remaining zones keep serving. A stateful tier uses a managed database in its high-availability configuration: Cloud SQL HA keeps a primary and a standby in two zones of one region, replicates writes synchronously, and promotes the standby on failure with a short interruption, without a restore step. The standby does not serve reads. Match the design to the requirement: For a target like EHR Healthcare's 99.9% for customer-facing systems, a few minutes of database interruption is tolerable and multi-region cost is unneeded, so regional MIG plus Cloud SQL HA fits. Multi-region is a separate, costlier step that protects against losing a whole region, which was not requested. Live migration handles host maintenance, not zone loss, and a zonal group with snapshots means manual recovery.

concepts.heading: Scaling Out, Not Up
concepts.body: The reliability and performance pillars favor scaling out (more instances) over scaling up (bigger ones). A larger VM has a ceiling, needs a restart to resize and remains a single point of failure. Scaling out works only if any instance can serve any request, so state must be externalized. Suppose a retailer like Cymbal Retail, which already runs Redis, keeps each cart in the memory of the VM that served the first request and uses session affinity; before a peak the fix is to move carts to a shared store such as Memorystore for Redis, make the web VMs stateless, and run them in an autoscaled managed instance group. Then a lost VM loses no carts, affinity is unnecessary, and capacity shrinks after the peak, which also cuts cost. Databases scale differently. Relational reads scale with Cloud SQL read replicas, which receive changes asynchronously and serve read-only queries while the primary keeps writing; they suit read-heavy workloads where slightly stale data is acceptable and need only a routing change in the application. They do not raise write throughput. A cache helps repeated lookups, and only when writes must scale globally with strong consistency does Spanner justify an engine change.

concepts.heading: Performance and Latency Design
concepts.body: Latency has several sources and the architect must diagnose which one applies before choosing a fix. Distance: round trips across continents cannot be bought away with faster servers, so content must move closer to users. Suppose an Altostrat-style media service serves viewers on several continents from one region while the origin is lightly loaded; a global external Application Load Balancer with Cloud CDN caches popular episodes at edge locations, cutting start-up time and offloading the origin. A dual-region bucket would improve durability, not distance. Compute startup: serverless services such as Cloud Run scale to zero, and the first request after idle waits for a new instance (a cold start). Setting minimum instances keeps warm capacity for latency-sensitive paths at a small continuous cost, with autoscaling above it; this is far cheaper than a fixed fleet sized for bursts. Data access: read replicas or a cache relieve a saturated primary. Entry point: a global load balancer routes to the nearest healthy region. Always check where the time goes: adding vCPUs to a lightly loaded origin does nothing for a latency problem that comes from network distance.

concepts.heading: Graceful Degradation and Gemini Cloud Assist
concepts.body: High availability is not only about replicas; it is also about how one failing part is allowed to affect the rest. The reliability pillar lists graceful degradation: when a non-essential dependency fails, lose that feature, not the whole function. Classify dependencies as hard (checkout, payment) or soft (recommendations, banners), give hard ones the stricter targets, and protect against soft ones with short timeouts, circuit breakers that stop calling a failing dependency for a while, and fallbacks such as cached or default content. Unbounded retries are the opposite: they add load to an already struggling service and can turn a partial failure into a full outage. Gemini Cloud Assist is the AI collaborator in Google Cloud that supports the lifecycle: design and build (natural-language architecture design, Terraform and gcloud generation), support and troubleshoot (investigations that analyze logs, metrics and configurations to find root causes), and optimize (cost questions, proactive cost anomaly analysis, network flow and storage insights). Pick the feature by lifecycle phase and pillar, and remember its output is advice a person reviews, not an order.

examPoints: A question that needs zone-level resilience with minutes of database interruption and no multi-region budget points to a regional managed instance group plus Cloud SQL high availability.
A question where carts or sessions live in VM memory and traffic will spike is testing externalized state (Memorystore) with a stateless autoscaled group, not bigger machines.
A question where latency comes from viewer distance and the origin is lightly loaded points to Cloud CDN behind a global external Application Load Balancer, not more origin capacity.

quiz.q: A reservation site's checkout page calls a loyalty-points service to show a points balance. When that service slows down, checkout times out and bookings are lost, although the balance display is optional. Which change best follows reliability guidance?
choices: Add a short timeout and a circuit breaker to the loyalty call and render checkout without the balance when it fails
Retry the loyalty call until it succeeds, so that every page eventually shows the correct balance to the customer
Give the loyalty service the same availability target as the booking path so that it can never become the bottleneck
Remove the points balance from the checkout page permanently so that the page no longer depends on that service
quiz.explain: Graceful degradation keeps the revenue path alive by letting the soft dependency fail with a timeout, breaker and fallback. Unbounded retries are tempting but pile load onto the struggling service and slow the page further.

quiz.q: A news company runs a stateless API on a regional managed instance group in one region. Its single Cloud SQL primary hits its CPU limit at peak, 85% of queries are read-only lookups, and the team does not want to change database engines. Which action scales with least change?
choices: Migrate the database to Spanner so that both reads and writes scale horizontally across several regions
Turn off high availability on the primary so that the standby no longer consumes any of its resources
Add Cloud SQL read replicas and route read-only queries to them, while writes keep going to the primary
Move the nightly report job into the maintenance window so that it no longer competes with live queries
quiz.explain: Read replicas offload reads with only a connection-routing change. Spanner is tempting for scale, but the workload is read-heavy and the team ruled out a new engine; the HA standby serves no queries, so turning it off frees no CPU for reads.

days.recap: Use the six pillars to see which requirement an answer serves; survive zone loss with regional MIGs and Cloud SQL HA, scale out with stateless tiers and read replicas, fix distance with Cloud CDN and cold starts with minimum instances, and degrade softly with timeouts and breakers.

days.title: Backup, Recovery, RTO and RPO, DR Patterns and Availability Math

concepts.heading: Availability Math for Dependent Components
concepts.body: An availability promise applies to what the customer experiences, which is the whole request path. When components are called in series and all must work, their availabilities multiply, so the chain is less available than its weakest member. A web tier, an API tier and a database at 99.9% each give roughly 99.7% end to end. This is why EHR Healthcare cannot repeat a 99.9% promise to hospitals just because each component has a 99.9% objective. The architect has three levers. Tighten the targets of critical dependencies. Add redundancy so that a single component failure does not fail the request: redundant copies in parallel fail only when all copies fail together, so two independent 99.9% copies in parallel are far better than one. Reduce hard serial dependencies, for example by making non-essential calls asynchronous or optional. Also remember what redundancy does not cover: independent failure is the assumption, so copies in the same zone, or behind the same single load balancer or configuration, share a failure domain. Spread redundancy across zones or regions according to the failure you must survive.

concepts.heading: RTO, RPO and the Cost Curve
concepts.body: DR is a subset of business continuity planning and begins with a business impact analysis that defines the RTO, the maximum acceptable time the application can be offline, and the RPO, the maximum acceptable window during which data might be lost. The smaller these values, the more the application costs to run and the more complexity and administration it brings. RTO and RPO roll up into service level objectives, which are measurable elements of an SLA. Read the numbers literally. A 15-minute RPO is far smaller than any nightly backup interval, so data must be replicated continuously, for example through a cross-region read replica that can be promoted. A 4-hour RTO leaves time to scale out a prepared stack, so a full hot environment is unnecessary. HA is related but different: it keeps an agreed level of uptime and often fixes RTO and RPO inside a region, while DR addresses a larger event such as the loss of a region. Choose the cheapest pattern whose replication meets the RPO and whose recovery steps fit within the RTO.

concepts.heading: DR Patterns: Backup, Pilot Light, Warm Standby and Hot
concepts.body: Google's disaster recovery planning guide describes patterns as cold, warm or hot, using a flat-tire analogy. Cold means no spare: minimal resources exist in the recovery location, and recovery means provisioning and restoring from backups, so RTO is long and RPO equals the age of the last backup. This suits historical compliance data. Warm means data is continuously replicated and a reduced-size environment is running or ready; on failover you scale it up, so RTO is shorter without paying for full capacity. Hot means both environments serve production traffic, giving the smallest RTO and RPO and the highest cost, which fits a critical online service. Pilot light, as the bank's DR questions use it, is a low-cost variant on this scale: the continuously replicated data layer runs in the recovery location while compute is defined as code and started only after a disaster is declared, so it recovers more slowly than warm standby and costs less. Read the stem's RTO and RPO rather than the label. A logistics company with an RTO of 4 hours, an RPO of 15 minutes and no budget for a second production stack is a warm standby: cross-region replica plus a scaled-down copy of the stack.

concepts.heading: Redundancy Is Not Backup
concepts.body: High availability and replicas protect against loss of infrastructure: an instance, a zone or a region. They also copy every change, including a wrong one. A dropped table, a bad UPDATE or an encrypting attacker is replicated to the standby and the replica within seconds, so a bigger machine, another replica or a faster failover restores nothing. Protection against logical damage needs an earlier state. In Cloud SQL, automated backups plus point-in-time recovery restore to a chosen timestamp just before the faulty statement. For ransomware and malicious deletion, Backup and DR Service stores policy-based backups in a backup vault with write-once-read-many immutability and indelibility, so a compromised account cannot remove them. Cloud Storage adds Object Versioning for older generations and retention policies to block deletion for a period, but neither speeds up replication. Replication is also not a full BCDR plan on its own. A sound design combines both: HA and replicas for availability, immutable and point-in-time backups for recovery from corruption, and tested restores to prove the backups work.

concepts.heading: Making Recovery Real: Capacity, Fail-over and Replication Targets
concepts.body: A DR design fails in practice at details the diagram hides. Capacity: a recovery environment needs its resources at the time of the disaster, and in a regional event many customers start resources at once. If the RTO depends on scaling up to production size, secure Compute Engine capacity with reservations in the recovery region and keep the rest elastic; rehearsals find such gaps early. Entry point: DNS-based fail-over depends on resolver caching and on someone noticing, so users can keep reaching a failed region for an hour. A global external Application Load Balancer has one anycast address and health-checks backends in every region, routing around a failed region automatically; the data layer must still fail over too. Data: a Cloud Storage dual-region bucket fails over automatically with no path changes, but replication is asynchronous; default replication targets 99.9% of new objects within an hour and all within 12 hours, while turbo replication targets a 15-minute RPO. Finally, access: make sure users and operators can sign in to the DR environment, and include them in regular DR tests.

examPoints: A question that states three serial 99.9% components and promises 99.9% is testing that serial availabilities multiply, so the combined figure is lower and redundancy or stricter targets are needed.
A question where the standby and replica already show a dropped table is testing that replication copies mistakes; the answer is point-in-time recovery and immutable backups in a vault.

A question where a warm-standby scale-up failed because machines were unavailable in the recovery zone points to Compute Engine reservations, and one about a 15-minute RPO on a dual-region bucket points to turbo replication.

quiz.q: An insurer's claims system needs an RTO of 2 hours and an RPO of 5 minutes if its primary region is lost. Finance will not fund a duplicate production environment that serves traffic all the time. Which pattern fits?
choices: Cold recovery from nightly backups copied to another region, with the stack built from templates after a disaster
Hot active-active deployment in two regions, with both environments serving production traffic at full capacity
Zone-redundant deployment in the primary region, with a regional load balancer spreading traffic over all its zones
Warm standby with a continuously replicated cross-region database and a scaled-down stack that is scaled up on failover
quiz.explain: Continuous replication meets the 5-minute RPO and a prepared, scaled-down stack can be expanded inside 2 hours without full duplicate cost. Cold recovery is tempting for cost, but nightly backups imply up to a day of data loss.

quiz.q: A team runs Cloud SQL with high availability and a cross-region replica. At 10:05 a developer's script deletes rows from a customer table, and the team notices at 10:30. The standby and the replica already lack the rows. What restores the data with least loss?
choices: Fail over to the standby, because it is a complete copy of the primary in a second zone of the region
Restore the instance to a point in time shortly before 10:05 using backups and point-in-time recovery
Promote the cross-region replica, because it is geographically separate from the primary instance and unaffected
Increase the machine size of the primary, because a larger instance makes the failover faster and safer
quiz.explain: Only an earlier state brings the rows back, and point-in-time recovery provides it. Promoting the replica is tempting because it is in another region, but it applies the same deletes as the primary.

days.recap: Serial availabilities multiply; set RTO and RPO from a business impact analysis, pick the cheapest cold, warm or hot pattern that fits, remember replicas copy mistakes so PITR and immutable vault backups are needed, and secure capacity, global fail-over and replication targets.

days.title: Choosing Network and Compute: Hybrid Links, VPC Models, GKE, Cloud Run and Compute Engine

concepts.heading: Choosing Hybrid Connectivity
concepts.body: The choice among hybrid links is driven by throughput, latency stability, the availability target and whether traffic may use the public internet. HA VPN builds IPsec tunnels over the internet: quick to set up and encrypted, but throughput per tunnel is limited and latency varies with internet conditions. Dedicated Interconnect is a physical connection at a colocation facility; traffic stays off the internet and capacity is dedicated, which suits sustained bulk transfers. Partner Interconnect reaches Google through a service provider when you cannot be in a Google colocation facility. Availability is a topology decision, not just a product decision: the documented 99.99% critical-production pattern uses at least four Dedicated Interconnect connections, two in one metro and two in another, with each pair in different edge availability domains. Maintenance is coordinated inside a metro but not across metros, so two metros keep one path alive. Altostrat Media needs secure, high-performance connectivity to ingest large media from legacy on-premises systems, with reliability a top priority, so redundant Dedicated Interconnect across two metros fits. One connection with a VPN backup, or one HA VPN pair, does not meet that.

concepts.heading: VPC Sharing Models: Shared VPC, Peering and Private Service Connect
concepts.body: Three models connect networks, each answering a different question. Shared VPC lets one organization connect resources from many projects to a single VPC network in a host project; the network team owns subnets, routes and firewall rules; service-project teams may only use specific subnets. It fits a retail group with many product teams needing central control and internal-IP communication. VPC Network Peering joins two separately administered VPC networks so they exchange routes privately; each side keeps its own administration, peering is not transitive and ranges must not overlap, so it suits independent networks, even across organizations. Private Service Connect (PSC) is service-oriented: a producer publishes a service through a service attachment, and each consumer creates an endpoint, an internal IP address in its own VPC that forwards to the service. Consumers reach only the published service, not the producer's network; overlapping ranges do not matter. A vendor serving many customer VPCs with overlapping ranges should use PSC. Network Connectivity Center adds a hub-and-spoke model where Interconnect, VPN and router appliance spokes exchange site-to-site traffic over Google's network, as with a manufacturer's plants.

concepts.heading: Reaching Google APIs Privately
concepts.body: Security rules often say machines may have no external IP addresses, yet they must call Google APIs such as Cloud Storage and BigQuery without crossing the public internet. Private Google Access lets VMs in a subnet that have only internal addresses reach Google APIs and services. Private Google Access for on-premises hosts extends this to servers, with or without external IPs, through a Cloud VPN tunnel or Interconnect VLAN attachment, using special Private Google Access domains and virtual IP addresses, with DNS and routes pointing to them. Private Service Connect for Google APIs is an alternative that uses an endpoint with an internal IP address in your VPC. Cloud NAT is different: it lets resources without external IPs open outbound connections to the internet, but it does not give API-private access. The design question is always which path the traffic takes and who owns the address space. These choices belong in the architecture because they interact with firewall policy, DNS and IP planning, and fixing them after workloads are deployed means changing routes and addressing under load.

concepts.heading: Choosing Compute: From Functions to Virtual Machines
concepts.body: Matching compute to the workload shape follows one principle: the more of the stack the platform runs, the less you operate. Cloud Run functions run single-purpose code triggered by events such as a Cloud Storage object change, a Pub/Sub message or an HTTP call, scale to zero and need no servers; Altostrat's metadata extraction on each new video is the textbook case. Cloud Run runs any stateless container as a service or job, also scaling to zero, when you need a custom runtime or a whole web application. GKE runs Kubernetes for complex multi-service platforms needing cluster-level control. In Autopilot mode GKE manages nodes and many best practices and is recommended for most production workloads, but it limits node access, so privileged DaemonSets or kernel settings call for Standard mode, where you control node pools and configuration. Compute Engine gives VMs and OS-level control, and is the choice for lifted-and-shifted software, special licensing or machine shapes. EHR Healthcare's several clusters across Google Cloud and on-premises benefit from fleets and GKE Enterprise for consistent configuration, policy and visibility, which addresses past outages caused by misconfiguration.

concepts.heading: Cost-Shaping Compute: Spot, Custom Shapes and Commitments
concepts.body: After choosing the platform, shape the cost. Spot VMs are excess capacity at a large discount, but Compute Engine can preempt them at any time and they carry no SLA. They suit interruption-tolerant work such as batch, rendering, simulation and CI. Design rules: make jobs short and idempotent or checkpoint progress, use a managed instance group or batch scheduler so replacements appear automatically, and allow several machine types so capacity is easier to find. Autonomous-driving simulation runs like KnightMotives', where a failed run can restart, are a good fit; a stateful or latency-critical service is not, and Spot for a shopping cart on the busiest day loses carts. A custom machine type lets you pick vCPU count and memory within allowed ratios for supported series, so a vendor requirement of 8 vCPUs and 40 GB does not force paying for an oversized predefined shape. For steady, predictable usage, add committed use discounts: right-size first, then commit. Oversizing for hypothetical growth wastes money, because resizing later is quick. Each step in this ladder is a trade between flexibility and price, and the stem tells you which side the business values.

examPoints: A question about reliable, off-internet bulk ingestion with a critical availability target points to redundant Dedicated Interconnect across two metros, because availability is a topology decision.

A question where one organization wants central network ownership with teams deploying into approved subnets points to Shared VPC, while overlapping ranges and a published service point to Private Service Connect.
A question about privileged node agents or kernel settings on Kubernetes points to GKE Standard, and interruption-tolerant batch with the lowest cost points to Spot VMs with restartable jobs.

quiz.q: A public-sector agency has three sites, each already linked to Google Cloud by Interconnect or HA VPN. The sites must exchange files with each other and with workloads in a hub VPC, and the agency does not want to buy a separate wide-area backbone. Which design fits?
choices: Attach the Interconnect and VPN connections as spokes to a Network Connectivity Center hub with site-to-site data transfer
Create VPC Network Peering between the sites, so that each site network can exchange routes with all of the others
Use Cloud NAT in each site, so that every site can open outbound connections to every other site and the hub
Publish each site as a Private Service Connect service, so that the other sites consume it through endpoints
quiz.explain: A Network Connectivity Center hub with the links as spokes lets the sites exchange traffic over Google's network. Peering is tempting because it connects networks privately, but it joins VPC networks, not physical sites.

quiz.q: A media archive team runs a transcoding queue where each job takes a few minutes, can be restarted from scratch and runs overnight. They want the lowest compute cost and are happy to let a scheduler replace lost machines. Which choice fits?
choices: Standard VMs with a three-year resource-based commitment sized for the peak number of overnight jobs
A GKE Autopilot cluster with always-on nodes sized for the peak, so that no job is ever interrupted
Spot VMs in a managed instance group that allows several machine types and replaces preempted instances
A single large VM with live migration enabled so that the host never interrupts any running job
quiz.explain: Restartable, interruption-tolerant batch work is the Spot use case, and a managed group replaces lost capacity. The three-year commitment is tempting for savings, but it pays for peak capacity that sits idle for most of the day.

days.recap: Hybrid links: Interconnect for reliable bulk, topology sets availability. Shared VPC for central control, peering for independent networks, PSC for published services, NCC for site-to-site. Pick compute by how much you want to operate; Spot for restartable work, custom shapes and commitments for steady load.

days.title: Choosing Storage and Data Processing: Object, File, Block, Databases, Streaming and Spark

concepts.heading: Object, File and Block Storage
concepts.body: Start the storage decision from the access semantics the application needs. Object storage (Cloud Storage) holds immutable objects accessed through APIs and scales to huge archives; Cloud Storage FUSE can mount a bucket as a file system, but it does not offer full POSIX semantics, so applications that rely on in-place edits and file locking can behave differently. File storage (Filestore) provides managed NFS shares with POSIX semantics that many VMs mount at once, which is what a lifted-and-shifted application expecting a shared file system with locking needs when it cannot be changed. Block storage (Persistent Disk, Hyperdisk, Local SSD) attaches to VMs; standard disks are normally read-write on one VM, and read-write multi-attach is limited to specific disk types and needs a cluster-aware file system. The common exam trap is to pick the cheapest or most familiar service for a workload whose semantics it does not provide: a bucket for shared POSIX files, or a disk for data many hosts must write. Name the semantics first (object, shared file, block), then consider performance, durability and cost.

concepts.heading: Cloud Storage Location Types and Autoclass
concepts.body: Bucket location decides availability and data placement. A regional bucket stores data in one region at the lowest cost with no cross-region protection by itself. A dual-region bucket stores data redundantly in a specific pair of regions you choose, gives higher availability, replicates asynchronously, and fails over and back automatically with no change to storage paths. A multi-region bucket spreads data over a large geographic area such as the EU, with locations chosen by Google, so you cannot restrict it to two named regions. A financial service whose rules require two specific European regions and survival of a regional failure therefore needs dual-region, with turbo replication if the RPO for new writes must be short and predictable (a 15-minute target). Storage class is a separate dimension that trades lower storage price against retrieval cost and minimum storage durations, and it does not change availability, which follows the location. Lifecycle rules move or delete objects by conditions you define and suit predictable access. Autoclass moves objects to colder classes when unused and back to Standard when read, which fits a growing media archive like Altostrat's, where an old episode can become popular again.

concepts.heading: Choosing a Database
concepts.body: Pick the database from the data model, consistency need and scale pattern. Cloud SQL is a managed relational service for MySQL, PostgreSQL and SQL Server; Google handles patching, backups and failover, and HA keeps a standby in another zone. It is the lowest-effort target for a team moving SQL Server with T-SQL features and zonal fail-over. AlloyDB is a managed PostgreSQL-compatible service for demanding transactional and analytical workloads. Spanner is relational with SQL and ACID transactions, scales horizontally, and in multi-region configurations replicates synchronously with strong consistency and keeps serving after a regional loss; it uses GoogleSQL or PostgreSQL dialects, not T-SQL, so applications change. A global ticketing platform accepting writes on three continents is the Spanner case. Bigtable is a wide-column NoSQL store for very high throughput, low-latency key access; row key design is the main decision, such as a device identifier followed by a timestamp for sensor data. It replicates asynchronously and has no multi-row relational transactions. Firestore is a document database, Memorystore is an in-memory cache, and Compute Engine VMs give full control while you own patching, backups and failover.

concepts.heading: Streaming and Batch Data Processing
concepts.body: A common streaming architecture has three parts. Pub/Sub decouples producers from consumers and absorbs bursts. Dataflow is the fully managed service for Apache Beam pipelines, batch and streaming, which autoscales workers and handles windowing and retries, so nobody sizes a cluster. BigQuery is the analytics warehouse, with rows queryable within seconds through the Storage Write API or streaming inserts. EHR Healthcare, ingesting data from new providers with unpredictable spikes and needing records cleaned within seconds, fits this pattern. Managed Service for Apache Spark (formerly Dataproc) fits when you already have Spark or Hadoop jobs to migrate with little change; for new continuous pipelines without cluster management, Pub/Sub plus Dataflow is the managed answer. BigQuery itself covers large-scale SQL analytics and often removes the need for a separate processing engine. The deciding facts are existing code, latency target, and how much infrastructure the team wants to run. For file-oriented transfers, the loading step into the warehouse can be a scheduled load job instead of streaming.

concepts.heading: Managed Domain Services and Build versus Buy
concepts.body: When a managed, domain-specific product exists, it normally beats a custom build on time to value and operations. Cymbal Retail wants natural-language product search ranked by catalog and shopper behavior; AI Commerce Search (in Gemini Enterprise for Customer Experience) ingests the catalog and user events and serves search and recommendations through APIs, whereas assembling the same from general parts means writing and tuning ranking, query understanding and an event pipeline. Document AI processors parse fixed-layout forms into structured fields with confidence scores; because its built-in Human in the Loop feature was deprecated, a review step is built in the application by routing low-confidence documents to a reviewer. In a storage and processing design the same logic applies: choose managed services over self-run clusters unless an existing investment, a special licence, or a control requirement says otherwise. Balance each choice against the stated priority: reliability and cost for Altostrat, compliance for EHR Healthcare, growth and lower cost for Cymbal. The architect's answer states why the chosen service fits the requirement, not merely that it works.

examPoints: A question about an unchangeable application needing a shared file system with locking points to Filestore managed NFS, not a Cloud Storage bucket.

A question that needs a short, unpredictable-access archive cost reduction without lifecycle guesswork points to Autoclass, and one needing two named European regions with regional-failure survival points to a dual-region bucket.

A question about worldwide writes with strong consistency points to Spanner, while huge key-based time-series throughput points to Bigtable and bursty streaming into BigQuery points to Pub/Sub plus Dataflow.

quiz.q: A telematics company stores GPS pings from two million vehicles, each sending a small record every few seconds. The application looks up a vehicle's recent track by key and needs very low latency at high sustained write rates; no joins are required. Which store fits?
choices: Cloud SQL with a read replica, because SQL queries are easiest for analysts to write and maintain
A Cloud Storage bucket with one object per ping, because object storage scales to any volume of data
Bigtable with a row key that starts with the vehicle identifier followed by the timestamp
Spanner in a multi-region configuration, because it always provides the strongest consistency in any case
quiz.explain: Bigtable is built for high write throughput and low-latency key lookups, and a vehicle-plus-timestamp key keeps a track together. Spanner is tempting for its scale, but the workload needs no relational transactions or global consistency, so its cost and complexity are unjustified.

quiz.q: An analytics team has a large set of existing Spark jobs on an on-premises Hadoop cluster and wants to move them to Google Cloud quickly, with minimal rewriting of the code. Which choice fits?
choices: Run Managed Service for Apache Spark, formerly Dataproc, so existing Spark jobs run with little change
Rewrite every job as an Apache Beam pipeline on Dataflow before moving, so that no cluster exists
Convert the jobs into Cloud Run functions, because functions remove any need for processing capacity
Load the raw data into a Filestore share and let analysts run the jobs from their desktops
quiz.explain: Existing Spark and Hadoop jobs are the case for Managed Service for Apache Spark. A Dataflow rewrite is tempting because it is fully serverless, but it delays the move and adds risk when the requirement is minimal rewriting.

days.recap: Name the storage semantics first (object, NFS, block); location decides availability, class decides price, Autoclass removes access guessing; Cloud SQL for easy relational, Spanner for global strong consistency, Bigtable for key-based scale; Pub/Sub plus Dataflow plus BigQuery for streaming; managed Spark for existing Spark.

days.title: Choosing AI and ML Solutions, and Starting Migration Planning with Migration Center

concepts.heading: Choosing Between Task-Specific AI and General Models
concepts.body: Google Cloud offers prebuilt, task-specific AI services and general-purpose foundation models, and the architect's job is to match the problem. Document AI provides processors that parse documents into structured fields with confidence scores, including processors for common forms and custom extractors; for thousands of scanned loan applications with fixed layouts and a need to route low-confidence results to a human, the specialised processor is the better-governed choice. Gemini models, reached through the Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform (formerly Vertex AI), are general multimodal models that read documents and varied inputs flexibly, but they need prompt design and evaluation. Custom model training is warranted only when no prebuilt option reaches the quality you need. AI Commerce Search is a managed product for retail search and recommendations. The decision rule: use the most managed, most specific capability that meets the quality bar, and move toward general or custom models only for flexibility, unusual data or differentiation. The same pillars apply: reliability (evaluation and fallbacks), cost (tokens, accelerators), security (data handling), and operational excellence (monitoring and versioning).

concepts.heading: Grounding, Agent Search and Agents
concepts.body: Foundation models generate plausible text from patterns learned in training; they do not know a company's current catalog and can invent details, called hallucination. Grounding supplies trusted data at answer time: the system retrieves relevant passages from your own documents (retrieval-augmented generation, RAG) and the model answers from them, often with citations. On Google Cloud you can assemble this from managed parts: a foundation model from the Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform or Model Garden, Agent Search for retrieval over your content, and Conversational Agents or an agent runtime for the chat interface. Altostrat Media wants a 24/7 viewer-support chat that answers only from its program guides and policies, cites sources and does not invent shows, so the design is grounding with retrieval over those documents plus a managed conversational layer. Fine-tuning changes behavior and style but is a poor way to keep facts current, and training from scratch is the most expensive option and is not justified. Model Garden is the place to discover and deploy Google, partner and open models when you need a choice of model.

concepts.heading: AI Infrastructure Choice: When to Use AI Hypercomputer
concepts.body: AI Hypercomputer is Google Cloud's integrated architecture for AI workloads: accelerators (GPUs and TPUs), high-bandwidth cluster networking, high-performance storage, and software and consumption options for large training and serving jobs. Choose it when you must train or heavily tune models yourself, such as a research lab pretraining a large custom model across hundreds of accelerators for weeks, which needs tight node-to-node communication that serverless request-based platforms and general-purpose VMs cannot provide. If you only use or lightly adapt an existing model, hosted models through the Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform or Model Garden are cheaper and faster to adopt. The architect also weighs governance: the Altostrat case asks for AI that is auditable and explainable, and Cymbal Retail needs a human-in-the-loop review interface before generated catalog attributes reach customers. Responsible-use controls, evaluation against supplier data, and monitoring belong in the design from the start, not as an afterthought. The exam asks for a sensible match between the need and the layer of the AI stack, not for model internals.

concepts.heading: Migration Planning Starts With Assessment
concepts.body: A migration plan starts from facts: what exists, how it is used, and what depends on what. Migration Center is the Google Cloud platform for the assessment and planning stages. Discovery gathers an inventory of servers and databases automatically or from uploaded data. Assessment maps application and network dependencies, gives target product suggestions based on a technical fit assessment, and produces total cost of ownership reports from the preferences you specify. Planning gives prescriptive recommendations, and the dependency results show which assets must move together, the basis for grouping them into waves. EHR Healthcare must leave a colocation facility whose lease is about to expire and has applications tied to on-premises insurer integrations; the right first step is discovery and dependency mapping, because moving things blindly would break integrations, while a full redesign of everything cannot fit before the lease ends. A fixed lease end makes ordering decisive, and most estates rehost first and modernize later. Spreadsheets of server lists are usually outdated, so automated inventory beats them.

concepts.heading: Migration Approaches and Waves
concepts.body: Google's migration guidance orders approaches from least to most change. Rehost (lift and shift) moves a workload with minor or no modification: quickest and uses existing skills, but it does not use cloud features such as horizontal scaling or managed services. Replatform (lift and optimize) adopts some cloud capabilities, for example containers or a managed database. Refactor or re-architect changes the workload to use cloud capabilities, such as splitting a monolith. Rebuild decommissions and rewrites as a cloud-optimized application. Repurchase replaces it with a SaaS equivalent. Rehost is right when change is impossible (no source code, vendor restrictions) or time leaves no room, and optimization follows later. Work is done in waves. The first wave is a pilot meant to validate the foundation, tooling and runbooks, so choose workloads that are low in criticality, simple in dependencies and representative; complex and critical systems move once the process is proven and dependency data is in hand. The cost of learning should be paid where failure is cheap, so a team inexperienced with the landing zone does not start with its most critical or most coupled application.

examPoints: A question about fixed-layout forms at volume with confidence scores and a human review step points to Document AI processors rather than a general model or custom training.

A question that wants a chat assistant to answer only from company content with citations and without inventing items points to grounding with retrieval (Agent Search) rather than fine-tuning or training from scratch.
A question with a fixed migration deadline and thin documentation points to Migration Center discovery and dependency mapping first, rehost first, and a low-risk, representative pilot wave.

quiz.q: A university research group wants to pretrain its own large model on proprietary data, running a distributed job across hundreds of accelerators for several weeks. Which infrastructure choice fits?
choices: Cloud Run functions, because their scaling to zero keeps the cost of the training job low between runs
AI Hypercomputer with GPUs or TPUs, high-bandwidth cluster networking and high-performance storage
A hosted Gemini model through Agent Platform, because it already contains everything the lab needs to train
A pair of Compute Engine VMs in one zone, because simple infrastructure is easier to manage than clusters
quiz.explain: Large distributed pretraining needs accelerators with fast node-to-node networking and storage, which AI Hypercomputer integrates. The hosted model is tempting because it is easy, but it is for using or lightly adapting a model, not pretraining your own.

quiz.q: A retailer will migrate 300 servers over a year. Its team has never built a landing zone or run cutover runbooks. Which application should go in the first wave?
choices: The order database that the whole business depends on, so the hardest case is proven first
The most tightly coupled application, so that every dependency pattern is learned in the first month
The application with the largest data volume, to test the migration tooling at its maximum scale
An internal, low-criticality application with few dependencies that resembles many later workloads
quiz.explain: A pilot should validate the foundation and runbooks on a representative system where failure is cheap. Starting with the critical database is tempting as a proof of strength, but mistakes there have a large business impact.

days.recap: Use the most specific managed AI that meets the quality bar, ground models with retrieval instead of fine-tuning facts, reserve AI Hypercomputer for training you own, and start migrations with Migration Center assessment, rehost-first when time is short, and a low-risk representative pilot wave.

days.title: Migration Plans, Testing, Network Planning, Future Improvements and Domain 1 Consolidation

concepts.heading: Landing Zone, Network Planning and Licenses
concepts.body: Migration guidance moves through assess, plan and build the foundation, deploy, and optimize. The foundation or landing zone holds what every workload needs: the resource hierarchy and policies, the identity and access model including how existing directory users reach Google Cloud, network design with address plan and hybrid connectivity, logging, monitoring and security controls, and a billing structure that maps costs to owners. Moving workloads first and fixing the foundation later means re-creating networks, permissions and projects with downtime and inconsistent controls. IP planning is the most expensive thing to retrofit: hybrid links exchange routes, so overlapping ranges make traffic drop or misroute. Inventory on-premises and other-cloud ranges, including those from acquisitions, allocate non-overlapping blocks with growth room, and include ranges for GKE Pods and Services and private service access. Licensing is a migration input too: check the metric (per core, processor, VM or user), whether bring-your-own-license is allowed and what hardware rules apply. Sole-tenant nodes provide hosts dedicated to your projects, helping meet dedicated-hardware and core-tracking requirements for per-core licences.

concepts.heading: Migration Plan Documents and Costs
concepts.body: A migration plan is a set of artifacts the team and the business can review: an inventory with owners, a dependency diagram grouping assets into waves, a target architecture with the landing zone, a network and address plan, a cutover and rollback runbook, a testing plan, and a business case. The business case must include one-time and transition costs, or it overstates savings: dual running until cutover and stabilization end, assessment and migration tooling, data transfer, testing and rehearsals, training, licensing changes, support contracts that cannot be cancelled early and decommissioning. Sunk costs do not change a forward decision, and cost figures should rest on measured utilization from the assessment rather than allocated sizes. Many VMs allocated 16 vCPUs average under 10% use; copying them one for one carries waste into the cloud bill, where you pay for configured resources. Right-size from evidence, with headroom, verify with owners, and adjust after cutover; resizing in the cloud is cheap. Finally include a retire decision: servers with near-zero use, no inbound connections and no owner are candidates, confirmed with owners before deleting.

concepts.heading: Workload Testing, Cutover and Decommissioning
concepts.body: Test before cutting over, and plan the way back. Latency-sensitive paths need testing across the hybrid link. Suppose KnightMotives moved its build-to-order front end to Google Cloud while the mainframe ERP stayed on premises, and pages became slow because each page made dozens of sequential calls over the link. Bandwidth is how much can travel at once; latency is the round trip, and chatty designs pay it per call, so adding capacity does not help. Dependency mapping shows what must move together; options are to move tightly coupled components in the same wave, to reduce chatter with an API layer that batches calls, asynchronous messaging or caching of reference data, and to test before cutover. After cutover comes a stabilization period with the new system carrying real traffic while the source stays available: define rollback criteria (error rates, data discrepancies, performance), keep the source usable and ideally in sync, and decommission on a schedule once criteria are met for the agreed time. Wiping the old servers on Monday removes the safety net when risk is highest; keeping them forever turns migration into permanent dual running.

concepts.heading: Future Improvements and Roadmaps
concepts.body: Planning improvements is an architecture task. Modernize incrementally: the strangler pattern puts a facade of APIs or a proxy in front of the legacy system and rebuilds one capability at a time, so each step is small, testable and reversible; KnightMotives' mainframe ERP and supply chain suit this better than a big-bang cutover that could halt plants. Extend pilots with gates: Cymbal Retail's gen AI descriptions need human-in-the-loop review, metrics such as accuracy against supplier data and rejection rate, wider categories only when targets are met, and early compliance involvement. Optimize continuously: Active Assist (Recommender) produces recommendations for idle resources, rightsizing and policy, as input to a decision that an owner confirms. Treat dependencies as having lifecycles: Container Registry shut down in favour of Artifact Registry and Deployment Manager reached end of support in favour of Infrastructure Manager or Terraform, so schedule migrations before deadlines. Preview features are for non-production evaluation; production adoption for a regulated workload waits for GA. Lock-in is a trade-off weighed by exit cost and probability, applied to components where both are high.

concepts.heading: Cloud-First, Prioritisation and Domain 1 in One Page
concepts.body: A cloud-first policy makes the cloud the default target and requires justification to do otherwise. It is a rule of thumb, not a guarantee: a hospital imaging system tied to a certified on-premises device and a tight latency link is a valid exception, recorded with its reason and a review date and given hybrid connectivity. Prioritise improvements by value, risk reduction and effort, measured pain such as incidents and lead time, and dependencies; technical debt carries interest. Use SLOs and error budgets to settle reliability versus features: with budget left, ship; with it nearly spent, invest in reliability. Sequence data and AI roadmaps from ingestion, to governance, analytics and prediction. For spiky traffic, matching capacity to demand through autoscaling or serverless beats discounts on a peak-sized fleet. Domain 1 in one page: quantify requirements; set RTO and RPO from impact; pick the cheapest design that meets the target; choose the right network, compute, storage and AI layer; assess before migrating; build the foundation first; migrate in tested waves with rollback; and improve on evidence from post-implementation reviews and telemetry, not opinion.

examPoints: A question about overlapping address ranges before hybrid connectivity is testing that IP planning must be done before the first subnet, because re-addressing live systems is a hard, expensive fix.

A question where pages are slow after splitting a chatty application across a hybrid link, with bandwidth to spare, is testing that latency per round trip matters, so batch, cache or move the components together.

A question about replacing a critical legacy system without halting operations points to the strangler pattern and incremental modernization, and a question about a Preview feature for a regulated workload points to non-production evaluation until GA.

quiz.q: A company completed cutover of its customer database to Google Cloud on Saturday. On Monday a manager proposes to power off and wipe the old on-premises servers to stop paying for them. What should the plan do instead?
choices: Run a stabilization period with agreed rollback criteria, keep the source usable, then decommission on a schedule
Wipe the servers on Monday, because keeping two copies of the data creates a risk of conflicting updates
Keep the servers for one year, because a rollback can never be ruled out as long as the company exists
Hand the servers to another team, because their reuse removes the need for a rollback or decommissioning plan
quiz.explain: A stabilization period with rollback criteria keeps the safety net while risk is highest and then retires the source on schedule. Wiping early is tempting for savings, but it removes the way back; keeping them for a year turns migration into permanent dual running.

quiz.q: A bank's board asks for a plan to replace a decades-old loan-servicing mainframe without any outage for branches. Which approach reduces risk most?
choices: A weekend big-bang cutover to a new platform after a short pilot, so that the legacy system is gone quickly
A lift and shift of the mainframe code to virtual machines, so that the design limits and debt are removed
An API facade in front of the mainframe, with capabilities rebuilt and switched over one at a time
Freezing the system and doing nothing until a vendor offers a ready-made replacement for the whole platform
quiz.explain: The strangler approach keeps each step small, testable and reversible while the facade routes traffic. Lift and shift is tempting because it removes the hardware, but it carries the technical debt and design limits forward unchanged.

days.recap: Build the landing zone and a non-overlapping IP plan first, include one-time and dual-running costs, right-size from measured use, test latency across hybrid links, keep rollback and decommission on schedule, then improve incrementally using evidence, SLOs and supported services.

days.title: Hybrid and Multicloud Connectivity: VPN, Interconnect Topologies, Cloud Router and Network Connectivity Center

concepts.heading: Picking the Link Type from the Requirements
concepts.body: Hybrid connectivity is chosen from four facts: how much sustained traffic, how stable the latency must be, how available the link must be, and whether traffic may cross the public internet. HA VPN builds IPsec tunnels over the internet. It is encrypted, fast to set up and cheap to start, but bandwidth per tunnel is limited and latency follows internet conditions, so it fits smaller flows, early migration phases and backup paths. Dedicated Interconnect is a physical connection between your network and Google at a colocation facility: private, predictable and suited to sustained bulk traffic. Partner Interconnect gives the same private path through a service provider when you cannot reach a Google facility or need less capacity. Cross-Cloud Interconnect links your VPC network to another cloud provider's network without your own colocation gear. Direct Peering and Carrier Peering exchange public traffic with Google's edge; they are not a private route into a VPC network. Altostrat Media, which moves audio and video from legacy ingestion systems, needs the private bulk option.

concepts.heading: Availability Is a Topology Decision
concepts.body: With Interconnect, the availability level comes from how many connections you order and where they sit, not from buying a bigger single link. The 99.9% configuration for non-critical applications uses two connections and two VLAN attachments in one metropolitan area, placed in different edge availability domains so that one maintenance event does not take both. The 99.99% configuration for critical applications uses four connections across two metros, with each pair in separate edge availability domains and attached through Cloud Routers in two regions. Maintenance is coordinated inside a metro but not across metros, which is why a second metro matters. You can mix Dedicated and Partner connections in a 99.99% design. HA VPN gets a 99.99% SLA for most topologies when both interfaces and tunnels are used, and it is a common backup for Interconnect. EHR Healthcare needs a secure high-performance link to insurers and a 99.9% availability goal for customer-facing systems: two connections in one metro would meet the connectivity floor, a four-connection design would suit its most critical paths.

concepts.heading: Cloud Router, BGP and Route Priority
concepts.body: Cloud Router is the managed BGP speaker for Cloud VPN, Cloud Interconnect and router appliances. It does not forward packets; it exchanges routes so that the VPC network learns on-premises prefixes as dynamic routes and on-premises learns your subnets. Three settings drive design. The VPC network's dynamic routing mode: regional advertises and learns only for the router's own region, global covers every region, so a multi-region design usually needs global. Advertisement mode: default advertises subnet ranges, custom lets you add or restrict prefixes, for example to summarize ranges. Priority: when the same prefix arrives over two paths, the lower value (MED) wins, so give the Interconnect a lower number and the VPN backup a higher one and the VPN carries traffic only when Interconnect routes disappear. Equal priorities allow ECMP-style sharing. BFD speeds up failure detection. KnightMotives, with plants that need reliable real-time connectivity, would keep an Interconnect primary and a VPN backup advertising the same prefixes with different priorities.

concepts.heading: Network Connectivity Center as the Hub
concepts.body: Once an organization has many VPC networks, branch offices and cloud providers, pairwise links turn into a mesh nobody can reason about. Network Connectivity Center (NCC) replaces it with a hub and spokes. The hub is a global resource; spokes are VPC networks, hybrid attachments (VPN tunnels, VLAN attachments), or router appliance VMs. VPC spokes exchange subnet routes through the hub, and hybrid spokes bring on-premises and other-cloud networks in, so every spoke can reach the others. With site-to-site data transfer, the hub lets external sites reach each other across Google's backbone, treating the VPC network as a WAN, though spokes using that feature must all sit in the same VPC network. The design question is operational: one place to see and change connectivity, instead of many peering and tunnel definitions. For Cymbal Retail, whose estate mixes on-premises sites, cloud workloads and Kubernetes clusters, an NCC hub with hybrid spokes is a cleaner target than a set of one-off VPN tunnels.

concepts.heading: Hybrid Design Checks Before Go-Live
concepts.body: A hybrid design fails more often on addressing and name resolution than on bandwidth. Subnet ranges must not overlap between VPC networks, on-premises networks and peered networks, which is why production uses custom mode VPC networks with planned ranges. Cloud DNS needs both directions: an inbound server policy so on-premises resolvers can query private zones in the VPC network, and a forwarding zone so VMs resolve corporate names on premises. Remember that firewalls act only after a route exists; a missing route looks like a firewall problem but no rule will fix it. Health checks from Google must be allowed by on-premises firewalls when on-premises backends sit behind a load balancer through a hybrid connectivity NEG. Encryption is a separate question: Interconnect is private but not encrypted by default, so regulated data may need HA VPN over Interconnect or MACsec where supported, plus TLS at the application. Finally, document the failure test: pull the primary and prove traffic moves to the backup within the target.

examPoints: Bulk, private, reliable hybrid traffic means Interconnect, and 99.99% needs four connections across two metros, not one bigger link.
In Cloud Router the lower priority (MED) value wins, so primary Interconnect gets the lower number and the VPN backup the higher one.
Many networks and sites that must reach each other call for a Network Connectivity Center hub with spokes rather than pairwise tunnels.

quiz.q: A hospital group runs its main data center in one city and must reach a Google Cloud VPC network for patient-record sync. The sync is business critical, has a stated 99.99% availability goal, and must stay off the public internet. Which design meets it?
choices: Two Dedicated Interconnect connections in the same metro on separate edge availability domains, with an HA VPN tunnel pair as a second path
Four Interconnect connections across two metros, each pair in separate edge availability domains, with Cloud Routers in two regions
One Dedicated Interconnect connection with a larger capacity and a Classic VPN tunnel kept as a manual standby for failures
HA VPN with two tunnels from one peer gateway and Direct Peering at a nearby edge location to carry the remaining bulk traffic
quiz.explain: The documented 99.99% topology is four connections over two metros with separate edge availability domains. Two connections in one metro reach only the 99.9% level, a single larger link is a single point of failure, and Direct Peering is not a private path into a VPC network.

quiz.q: A company's VPC network has an Interconnect and an HA VPN to the same data center, both advertising 10.20.0.0/16. Operations wants the VPN to carry traffic only when the Interconnect is down. What should the architect set?
choices: A higher route priority value on the Interconnect session than on the VPN session, so the VPN route is installed and used first
The same priority on both sessions, so that equal-cost paths share the load and the VPN absorbs any overflow when it is needed
A lower route priority value on the Interconnect session than on the VPN session, so the VPN route is used only after withdrawal
Regional dynamic routing on the VPC network and a separate Cloud Router for each path, so that the paths are chosen by region
quiz.explain: Lower values win, so the Interconnect must carry the lower number and the VPN the higher. Equal values give ECMP sharing, the reverse order would prefer the VPN, and the routing mode controls region scope, not path preference.

days.recap: Pick the link from throughput, latency stability, availability and exposure. Topology sets the SLA (99.99% = four connections, two metros); Cloud Router lower priority wins, so Interconnect primary, VPN backup; NCC is one hub for many networks; Interconnect is unencrypted by default (MACsec, HA VPN).

days.title: VPC Design, Firewalls, Load Balancing, Cloud NAT and Private Google Access

concepts.heading: VPC Network Design: Mode, Ranges and Sharing
concepts.body: A VPC network is global and its subnets are regional. Auto mode creates a subnet in every region from a predefined block, which is fine for experiments but can collide with on-premises or peered ranges, and it cannot be converted back once it is custom. Production uses custom mode with planned, non-overlapping ranges, because Cloud VPN, Interconnect and VPC Network Peering all need distinct addressing. For many teams, Shared VPC lets a host project own the network while service projects attach their workloads, so network administrators control subnets and firewalls centrally and application teams keep control of their own resources. Private Service Connect publishes or consumes a service through an internal endpoint, without peering whole networks together or sharing address space. Peering is not transitive, so a hub-and-spoke of peered networks does not give spokes reach to each other. The architect's rule: separate environments by project, centralize the network where one team owns policy, and decide the address plan before the first workload exists.

concepts.heading: Firewalls: Policies, Tags and Hierarchy
concepts.body: Cloud Next Generation Firewall (Cloud NGFW) evaluates rules in policies. Hierarchical firewall policies attach to the organization or a folder, and a rule can allow, deny or hand evaluation to the next level with goto_next, so a security team enforces non-negotiable rules such as blocking SSH from the internet while projects keep freedom for the rest. Network firewall policies attach to a VPC network. Rules can match on IP ranges, but identity-based matching is stronger: network tags are plain strings that anyone with permission to edit a VM can change, whereas secure tags are Resource Manager tags governed by IAM, so only the security team may create or bind them. Rules then follow workloads rather than addresses. Cloud NGFW Enterprise adds an intrusion prevention service: firewall endpoints in each zone inspect traffic that a rule sends to a security profile group, and can alert or deny. For EHR Healthcare's several Kubernetes environments, a hierarchical policy gives one consistent baseline, with secure tags separating database tiers.

concepts.heading: Detecting and Preventing Intrusions
concepts.body: Two services sit in different places in the traffic path. Cloud IDS mirrors traffic with Packet Mirroring to Google-managed inspection VMs through an IDS endpoint. Because it works on copies, it adds no latency and cannot break production, it sees east-west and intra-subnet traffic, and it detects and alerts but does not block. Cloud NGFW Enterprise intercepts matching packets inline, sends them to a zonal firewall endpoint and applies the action in the security profile, such as deny. The design choice is detection versus prevention: use IDS when the requirement is visibility and forensic evidence, add NGFW intrusion prevention when threats must be stopped, and send findings into Security Command Center or a SIEM so someone acts on them. Cloud Armor is the edge control for traffic entering through a load balancer, covering web application and DDoS protection; it does not inspect traffic between VMs in the same network. A layered answer on the exam often combines Armor at the edge, NGFW inside the network and IDS for monitoring.

concepts.heading: Choosing the Right Load Balancer
concepts.body: Select a load balancer by walking through four questions. Is the client external or internal? Which protocol: HTTP(S) or other TCP/UDP? Must the original client IP reach the backend without termination? Is it global or regional? A global external Application Load Balancer terminates HTTP(S) at Google's edge, offers one anycast address, URL-based routing, Cloud CDN and Cloud Armor, and fits public web apps and APIs, including Cloud Run through a serverless NEG. Regional external Application Load Balancers serve data residency needs. A proxy Network Load Balancer handles TCP with termination, and a passthrough Network Load Balancer does not terminate connections, preserving client IPs for TCP, UDP and other protocols in one region; a UDP game server is the textbook case. Internal Application Load Balancers serve private HTTP(S) services; a cross-region internal Application Load Balancer fails over between regions automatically, which suits an internal API that EHR Healthcare's tiers call from two regions behind one DNS name. Internal passthrough Network Load Balancers are regional. Hybrid NEGs let Application and proxy Network Load Balancers front on-premises backends.

concepts.heading: Reaching the Internet and Google APIs Privately
concepts.body: Private VMs and GKE nodes without external IP addresses still need controlled paths out. Cloud NAT translates outbound traffic for chosen subnet ranges on a regional gateway attached to a Cloud Router; it is software-defined with no proxy VMs and allows no unsolicited inbound connections. With automatic address allocation the address set can change, while manual allocation of reserved static addresses gives partners a stable list to allowlist, which Cymbal Retail's SFTP and batch supplier integrations would need. For private GKE clusters, include the Pod ranges. Private Google Access is a per-subnet setting that lets VMs with only internal addresses reach Google APIs and services; it does not reach third-party sites. On-premises hosts can reach Google APIs over Interconnect or VPN by using the private.googleapis.com or restricted.googleapis.com virtual IPs, where the restricted range pairs with VPC Service Controls. Private Service Connect endpoints for Google APIs are the more flexible modern alternative. The pattern is: Private Google Access for Google services, Cloud NAT for everything else outbound, load balancers for inbound.

examPoints: Use identity-based firewall matching (secure tags) when developers can edit VMs, and hierarchical policies for rules nobody below may override.
Cloud IDS detects through mirrored copies, while Cloud NGFW Enterprise intrusion prevention blocks inline.
Choose a load balancer by scope, protocol and whether the client IP must be preserved; passthrough keeps it, proxy balancers terminate.

quiz.q: A subscription video service runs a stateless public web API on Cloud Run and wants one global IP address, Cloud CDN for cached responses and Cloud Armor rules in front of it. Which front end should the architect choose?
choices: A regional external passthrough Network Load Balancer with the Cloud Run revisions registered as zonal instance group backends
A global external Application Load Balancer using a serverless network endpoint group that points at the Cloud Run service
A cross-region internal Application Load Balancer with global access enabled so clients in all regions can connect to it
A proxy Network Load Balancer for TCP with the Cloud Run service reached through a Private Service Connect endpoint
quiz.explain: Only the global external Application Load Balancer combines an anycast address, Cloud CDN and Cloud Armor, and a serverless NEG makes Cloud Run a backend. The passthrough and internal options lack those features and cannot front a public API this way.
